posts.author: jeff-blyth
posts.post_subject: Bayer and Ultimate joint agreement for color materials
posts.content_md:
> **Kaveh:** Sorry guys, let's try again:http://www.marketwatch.com/news/story/B ... 9B40393%7D

Hmmmm......one bIt says:

"By joining forces with UHR, we are working with one of the world's leading developers of full-color hologram technology and a company with extensive know-how in the production of holographic masters and mass replication," explains Dr. David Jurbergs, Holographic Application Development Manager at Bayer MaterialScience LLC. Peter Vivona, Vice President Marketing & Sales at UHR adds: "These photopolymers will enable us to produce full-color holograms on an industrial scale while also satisfying the strict requirements placed on commercial applications in terms of consistently high image quality and cost effectiveness." 

…. This upbeat assessment of mass producing color Denisyuk holograms 

seems to skate over that difficult issue that only we holographers know of. i.e. Except for coherence length , the reproduction will need the same exacting demands from a combination of 3 color lasers that had to be used to make the Ultimate master plates in the first place. But then maybe I am not keeping up with recent developments, perhaps there are sufficiently coherent sources of quasi-whitelight out there with only say 100 microns of coherence length that would be enough to do contact copies from Ultimate masters but there again the Bayer team would have to get the panchromatic sensitivity adjusted to suit the source …. quite difficult . Perhaps Ernest Hemingway might have put it like this:

“The road to holographic hell is paved with good intentions.”

By the way I have tested the Bayer prototype photopolymer (monochromatically) and it has quite astounded me. 

To get such good diffraction with a HeNe with no post processing and at exposure levels so amazingly low at 633nm for a photopolymer .---It has certainly made me lose sleep as I have been in this holographic non-silver halide recording game for over 20 years now. This stuff is quite fantastic and is likely to really change our little holography world for ever........ if it becomes generally available that is. 

Jeff

posts.topic_title: Bayer and Ultimate joint agreement for color materials
posts.author: jeff-blyth
posts.post_subject: Bayer and Ultimate joint agreement for color materials
posts.content_md:
> **Kaveh:** ................................................Jeff, this is very promising. What about sensitivity which has always been the issue? Did you get any feel for that?

Well I had only a very limited bit of material to try.

With a 15mw HeNe (roughly), I could get an amazingly bright result with only around 20 seconds exposure over an area of about 2 inches square. I was not able to get a handle on what happened with too much exposure. 

There is a fascinating side issue (for our future discussion here maybe), after about 10 seconds or so of exposure the light coming off the object goes into oscillation at a frequency around 10 hz. The effect is variable and not essential to a successful outcome. It also seems to be much more noticeable if you keep moving your head or viewing position--- it reminds me of seeing some bright object through a slatted fence.

What is the physics/chemistry going on here? 

Jeff

posts.author: jeff-blyth
posts.post_subject: Bayer and Ultimate joint agreement for color materials
posts.content_md:
> **BobH:** Perhaps you're seeing some real time interference between the object light and the image, which should be present in real time after a short time of exposure.

Yes, I guess you are on the right track. There is the question of a transport mechanism or diffusion going on. I know that a monomer

species as it polymerises increases its density (usually but not always) . An increase in density means a decrease in volume , that means the missing volume must draw in material from the dark fringe towards the developing light fringe and this process maybe going on on BOTH sides of the developing light fringe simultaneously therefore the spatial integrity between the developing fringes must be being maintained , --otherwise the fringe structure would self- destruct.

I have now managed to reproduce this effect now in my lab using a difunctional monomer and the dye methylene blue. So far the effect is not as strong as I have seen on the Bayer stuff and it is also very dependent on not having too much dye present.

Jeff

posts.content_md:
Hello Everyone,

Sorry it too me so long to get back to you about the poly I had another trip for the holidays.

At the Holopack conference in Toronto there was the Bayer Guy. David Jurbergs. He gave a speech about the stuff. This is a business conference so there was very little tech discussion going on. Jeff Blyth has already said more about using it than what was presented. I did get to see a half dozen or so pieces. It looked fine, I think they were all H2's, IP. The objects they used were mostly natural crystals. The lamination had lots of dust but thats not the fault of the material itself. 

It will be available in a year or two, he would not nail it down and it sounded like he really didn't know. It will be openly available, he did say that clearly. Only pre coated onto film. Bayer materials usually sells raw materials in 50 gal drums but Jurberg said it would be too hard for outsiders to coat it themselves. They would think about it for special cases and only for large users. Any companies like that would also have to be trained by Bayer. 

So, this is exactly what everyone is waiting for. Fast polycromatic volume stuff! Bright and easy to develop. A short wait but not too bad. 

 Jeffrey Weil

 NorthBeach Holography Inc.

For me personally , one of my hobbies is trying to understand how humans have evolved to be the way they are. I am particularly intrigued by the high proportion of inherent crooks and scamsters all around. Yes OK ,OK I’ll say it now to save you the bother------

“It takes one to know one”. Not unreasonably the largest proportion of Holography News is on the matter of the one big killer application of holography over the past 20 years ….anti-counterfeiting. If you are not interested in the arms race between counterfeiters and the fraud-prevention folk, then Holography World can be a bit of a lean read. However if one is interested then it can be stimulating to know what is working now, what is no longer working , and what may work for a while in the future. It is one small fascinating facet of the world-wide propensity for scams and deception.

Holograms are now on bank notes all over the world so we are talking about a very big money here . I. L’s comments on what is going on I find generally fair and perceptive.

Jeff
